material_systems.name: Alkali-Resistant Masonry Primer for Concrete Porch Floor

products: Benjamin Moore Ultra Spec Masonry & Stucco Primer
primer.notes: Mandatory on bare concrete substrate when coating_system = porch_enamel. New concrete pH 12-14 requires alkali-resistant primer — standard acrylic primer will fail via saponification. Coverage is lower on broom-finish concrete (200-250 SF/gal) vs troweled smooth (250-300 SF/gal). Not required for acrylic_sealer (self-priming) or concrete_stain (penetrating).

material_systems.notes: Reuses SYS_PRIMER_ALKALI_MASONRY concept from masonry spec. Porch floor concrete has same alkali chemistry as masonry walls. Coverage slightly lower than vertical masonry due to horizontal pooling tendency — maintain even application to avoid thick spots.

material_systems.name: Exterior Wood Primer for Wood Porch Floor

products: Benjamin Moore Fresh Start Exterior Primer
primer.notes: Required on bare wood porch floor when coating_system = porch_enamel. Seals wood grain, promotes adhesion, and provides uniform base for porch enamel finish. Coverage on dimensional lumber porch flooring (tongue-and-groove or decking boards) is consistent at 350-400 SF/gal. Mill glaze must be removed before priming.

material_systems.notes: Wood porch floors are typically tongue-and-groove fir, pine, or PT lumber. Primer adhesion is critical on horizontal walking surfaces subject to foot traffic and moisture exposure.

material_systems.name: Polyurea/Polyaspartic Basecoat Primer

primer.notes: Manufacturer-specific polyurea basecoat that bonds to profiled concrete and provides adhesion base for polyurea topcoat. Must be same manufacturer system as topcoat — cross-brand mixing PROHIBITED. Coverage depends on concrete profile and porosity. Requires mechanical profiling (diamond grind or shot blast) to CSP 2-3 for proper adhesion.

material_systems.notes: Polyurea systems are proprietary — primer and topcoat must be matched from the same manufacturer system. Concrete-only substrate. Fast cure (2-4 hours) enables same-day topcoat in favorable conditions.

material_systems.name: Moisture Vapor Barrier Primer (Contingency)

primer.type: Moisture mitigating epoxy primer / vapor barrier
primer.notes: Contingency primer triggered ONLY when moisture vapor emission rate (MVER) exceeds 5 lbs per 1000 SF per 24 hours, OR in-situ RH exceeds 85% (ASTM F2170). Applied BEFORE any other primer or coating. This is a hard stop override — if moisture test fails, this product is mandatory regardless of coating system. Epoxy-based, not acrylic.

material_systems.notes: Moisture testing per ASTM F1869 (calcium chloride) or ASTM F2170 (in-situ RH probe) is recommended on all concrete porch floors, especially slab-on-grade with no vapor barrier. If MVER/RH passes, this primer is not used. If it fails, this is applied first, then the standard primer system follows.

material_systems.name: Acrylic Porch & Floor Enamel

finish.type: Acrylic porch and floor enamel — abrasion-resistant floor coating
finish.notes: Primary floor coating for both concrete and wood porch substrates. Formulated for horizontal walking surface abrasion resistance. 2 coats mandatory for durability on traffic surfaces. Coverage varies by substrate: smooth troweled concrete 350-400 SF/gal, broom-finish concrete 300-350 SF/gal, wood flooring 350-400 SF/gal. Anti-slip aggregate broadcast into wet first coat.

material_systems.notes: Most versatile porch floor system — works on both concrete and wood. Satin is standard residential choice. Semi-gloss for maximum cleanability but shows wear patterns faster. Anti-slip aggregate is broadcast into the wet first coat before it skins over.

material_systems.name: Breathable Acrylic Concrete Sealer

sealer.type: Breathable acrylic concrete sealer — film-forming with vapor transmission
products: Euclid Euco Diamond Hard Acrylic Sealer
sealer.notes: Self-priming on properly profiled concrete — no separate primer required. Maintains concrete's natural appearance with slight sheen enhancement. Breathable formulation allows moisture vapor transmission, critical for exterior slab-on-grade applications. 2 coats for floor traffic durability. Anti-slip aggregate broadcast into wet first coat. Coverage depends on concrete porosity: dense troweled 250-300 SF/gal, broom finish 200-250 SF/gal.

material_systems.notes: Concrete-only system. Self-priming eliminates a material step but requires clean, profiled concrete surface. Acid etch or mechanical profiling mandatory for adhesion. Natural look option — tints available but color is translucent, not opaque like porch enamel.

material_systems.name: Penetrating Concrete Stain

stain.type: Penetrating concrete stain — acid-based or water-based reactive stain
stain.notes: Wide coverage range reflects fundamental chemistry difference: acid stain (100-200 SF/gal) reacts with calcium hydroxide in concrete to produce permanent color — coverage is porosity-dependent and lower. Water-based stain (200-300 SF/gal) deposits pigment into pores — more predictable coverage. Acid stain typically single application; water-based stain may require 2 coats for color intensity. MUST be sealed with SYS_EXT_PRFL_FINISH_SEALER_TOPCOAT after staining.

material_systems.notes: Concrete-only system. Acid stain produces mottled, variegated color unique to each pour — results are NOT uniform (this is the desired aesthetic). Water-based stain produces more uniform color. Both require sealer topcoat for UV protection and traffic durability. Acid stain requires neutralization rinse before sealer application.

material_systems.name: Clear Acrylic Topcoat Sealer (Over Concrete Stain)

sealer.type: Clear acrylic topcoat sealer — UV-stable, traffic-rated
products: SureCrete DK SureSeal Clear Acrylic Sealer
sealer.notes: MANDATORY topcoat over concrete stain — stain alone has no abrasion resistance or UV protection. 2 coats for traffic-rated durability on walking surfaces. First coat seals stain and builds base film; second coat provides wear surface. Anti-slip aggregate broadcast into wet first coat. Applied after stain has fully dried and any acid residue has been neutralized and rinsed.

material_systems.notes: Concrete-only system. Clear topcoat enhances stain color depth while providing traffic protection. Gloss option maximizes color enhancement (wet look) but shows wear patterns. Satin is standard for residential porch floors. Re-coat cycle: 2-4 years for traffic surfaces depending on exposure.

material_systems.name: Polyurea/Polyaspartic Floor Topcoat

finish.notes: Highest-performance floor coating system. UV-stable polyaspartic chemistry resists yellowing, chalking, and chemical attack. Extremely fast cure (4-6 hours walk traffic, 24 hours full cure). Coverage is lower than acrylic systems due to required film build (8-12 mils DFT). Must be same manufacturer as basecoat primer. Anti-slip aggregate broadcast into wet topcoat. Two-component product — pot life 15-30 minutes, must work quickly.

material_systems.notes: Concrete-only system. Premium performance tier — highest abrasion resistance, chemical resistance, and UV stability of all porch floor systems. Short pot life requires experienced applicator. Decorative flake/chip broadcast optional (not in v1 scope). Temperature-sensitive application: 50-90F.

coverage_profiles.description: Concrete substrate + porch enamel system (primer + 2 finish coats)

concrete_smooth.notes: Troweled or power-floated smooth concrete. Best primer coverage on concrete substrates.

concrete_broom.notes: Broom-finish concrete. Texture reduces coverage 15-20% vs smooth.

concrete_smooth.notes: Porch enamel on primed smooth concrete. Good film build on sealed surface.

concrete_broom.notes: Porch enamel on primed broom-finish concrete. Texture reduces coverage.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. 2 finish coats doubles finish material consumption.
Primer coverage assumes acid-etched or mechanically profiled concrete surface.
Anti-slip aggregate is broadcast into wet first finish coat — does not affect coverage rate but adds material cost.

coverage_profiles.description: Wood substrate + porch enamel system (primer + 2 finish coats)

wood_porch_floor.notes: Exterior wood primer on sanded porch flooring. Consistent coverage on dimensional lumber.
Porch enamel on primed wood flooring. Even absorption on sealed wood surface.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. 2 finish coats doubles finish material consumption.
Wood must be sanded (mill glaze removed) before priming.
Anti-slip aggregate is broadcast into wet first finish coat.

coverage_profiles.description: Concrete substrate + acrylic sealer system (self-priming, 2 coats)

concrete_smooth.notes: Acrylic sealer on smooth profiled concrete. Self-priming — no separate primer layer.

concrete_broom.notes: Acrylic sealer on broom-finish concrete. Texture increases absorption.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. 2 coats doubles material consumption.
Self-priming: no separate primer step required.
Concrete must be acid-etched or mechanically profiled for adhesion.
Anti-slip aggregate is broadcast into wet first coat.

coverage_profiles.description: Concrete substrate + concrete stain system (stain + sealer topcoat)

concrete_acid_stain.notes: Acid stain — reactive chemistry produces variable coverage. Highly porous concrete absorbs more. Single application typical.

concrete_water_based_stain.notes: Water-based concrete stain — pigment deposit, more predictable. 2 coats for full color intensity.

concrete_stained.notes: Clear topcoat sealer over stained concrete. Stain partially seals surface, improving topcoat coverage vs bare concrete.

assumptions: Coverage per coat for each layer.
Acid stain requires neutralization rinse (baking soda solution + water rinse) before sealer application.
Water-based stain coverage is more predictable than acid stain.
Anti-slip aggregate is broadcast into wet first sealer topcoat.

coverage_profiles.description: Concrete substrate + polyurea system (basecoat primer + topcoat)

concrete_profiled.notes: Polyurea basecoat on mechanically profiled concrete (CSP 2-3). Coverage varies by porosity and profile depth.
Polyurea topcoat — lower coverage due to required 8-12 mil DFT. Single coat standard; 2 coats for heavy traffic.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. Heavy traffic areas may require 2 topcoats.
Concrete must be mechanically profiled to CSP 2-3 (diamond grind or shot blast).
Anti-slip aggregate is broadcast into wet topcoat.
Two-component product — pot life 15-30 minutes constrains batch size.

consumables.name: Roller cover 3/8 inch nap (smooth concrete / wood floor)
consumables.notes: For porch enamel and acrylic sealer on smooth troweled concrete and wood flooring. 3/8 inch nap provides smooth finish appropriate for walking surfaces. 9-inch roller. Replace when nap becomes matted or loaded with aggregate.

consumables.name: Roller cover 1/2 inch nap (broom-finish concrete)
consumables.notes: For porch enamel and acrylic sealer on broom-finish concrete. 1/2 inch nap fills texture grooves. Standard concrete texture roller. Wears faster than smooth-surface rollers due to abrasive concrete texture.

consumables.name: Roller cover 3/4 inch nap (heavy broom-finish concrete)
consumables.notes: For heavy broom-finish or exposed aggregate concrete surfaces. 3/4 inch nap reaches into deeper texture grooves. Required when standard 1/2 inch nap does not achieve full coverage in texture valleys.

consumables.name: Brush 3-4 inch (edges, steps, detail)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 100 LF of edge cutting or 20 EA steps
consumables.notes: For cutting in edges where roller cannot reach: wall-to-floor junction, step nosings, post bases, expansion joints. Synthetic bristle for water-based products. 3-inch for detail work around posts/columns, 4-inch for long straight edges.

consumables.name: Roller frame 9 inch with extension pole
consumables.notes: Standard 9-inch roller frame with threaded extension pole for standing-height floor application. Extension pole eliminates bending — ergonomic requirement for floor coating. 4-6 ft pole standard for porch floors.

consumables.name: Paint tray or 5-gallon bucket with screen
consumables.notes: Standard paint tray for small areas (<200 SF) or 5-gallon bucket with roller screen for larger areas. Bucket method preferred for floor coating — holds more product, reduces refill frequency. Box multiple gallons for color consistency.

consumables.name: Pump sprayer (2-gallon, for acid stain application)
consumables.notes: Hand-pump sprayer for applying acid stain to concrete. Acid-resistant seals and gaskets required — standard pump sprayers will corrode. NOT airless spray — acid stain requires low-pressure even application. Also used for applying acid etch solution. Dedicate one sprayer to acid products, one to alkaline/neutral products.

consumables.name: Roller cover 3/16-1/4 inch nap (polyurea application)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 100-150 SF (disposable — fast cure hardens roller)
consumables.notes: Thin nap roller for polyurea/polyaspartic topcoat. Very short nap (3/16-1/4 inch) for thin-film, even application. DISPOSABLE — polyurea cures in roller within 30-45 minutes. Budget multiple roller covers per project. Lint-free synthetic only.

consumables.name: Painter's tape (exterior grade, UV-resistant)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 ROLL (60 yd) per 40 LF of masking lines
consumables.notes: UV-resistant exterior masking tape for masking wall-to-floor junction, railing bases, post bases, and expansion joint edges. 14-day removal rating minimum. Standard blue painter's tape. Reused consumable ID.

consumables.name: Masking paper (brown kraft or painter's paper)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 ROLL per 100 LF of wall base protection
consumables.notes: For protecting adjacent wall surfaces at floor-to-wall junction during roller application. Tape paper at wall base, extending 12-18 inches up wall to catch roller splatter. More effective than tape alone for floor coating splatter protection.

consumables.name: Plastic sheeting (4 mil, UV-resistant)
consumables.notes: For landscape/hardscape edge protection and covering adjacent surfaces. 4 mil minimum. UV-resistant for multi-day exterior projects. Used at porch perimeter where coating could drip onto landscaping, walkways, or driveway.

consumables.name: Canvas drop cloths
consumables.notes: For protecting adjacent walkways, steps, and hardscape from coating drip and roller splatter. Non-slip surface for crew traffic. Reused consumable ID.

consumables.name: Muriatic acid (31.45% HCl) for acid etch profiling
consumables.usage_rate: 1 GAL per 75-100 SF of concrete etch (diluted 1:3 to 1:4 with water)
consumables.notes: For acid etching concrete to achieve proper surface profile (CSP 2-3) for coating adhesion. Dilute 1:3 or 1:4 with water — ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid. Requires PPE: chemical-resistant gloves, splash goggles, acid-rated respirator. Neutralize with baking soda solution after etching, rinse thoroughly. Alternative: phosphoric acid (safer but slower).

consumables.name: Baking soda or TSP for acid neutralization
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA (5 lb box baking soda) per 200 SF acid-etched area
consumables.notes: For neutralizing muriatic acid etch residue on concrete. Dissolve baking soda in water, apply to etched surface, scrub, and rinse thoroughly. Surface pH must return to neutral (7-8) before coating. Also used for neutralizing acid stain residue. TSP is an acceptable alternative neutralizer.

consumables.name: Concrete patching compound (polymer-modified)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 QT per 20 LF of crack repair or 10 EA spall patches
consumables.notes: Polymer-modified concrete patching compound for filling cracks, spalls, and surface defects before coating. Must cure per manufacturer instructions (typically 24-48 hours) before acid etch or coating. Feather-edge patches for smooth transitions. Do not use standard Portland cement mortar — it does not bond well to existing concrete.

consumables.name: Sandpaper 60-80 grit (wood mill glaze removal)
consumables.notes: For removing mill glaze on new wood porch flooring before priming. 60 grit for initial glaze breakthrough, 80 grit for smoothing. Random orbital sander or belt sander. Wood substrate only — not used on concrete.

consumables.name: Chemical mill glaze remover
consumables.usage_rate: 1 GAL per 200 SF of wood floor treatment
consumables.notes: Alternative to mechanical sanding for mill glaze removal on new wood porch flooring. Apply, allow dwell time per product instructions, rinse. Less aggressive than sanding — does not alter wood profile. Preferred method when preserving original board surface is desired. Wood substrate only.

consumables.name: Silica sand 30-60 mesh (anti-slip aggregate for level surfaces)
consumables.usage_rate: 1-2 LB per 100 SF of floor area
consumables.notes: MANDATORY anti-slip aggregate for all coating systems on level porch floor surfaces. Broadcast into wet first coat of finish/sealer/topcoat before skinning occurs. 30-60 mesh provides traction without excessive roughness for bare feet. Clear coatings: use fine mesh (60) to minimize visual impact. Pigmented coatings: standard mesh (30-40) acceptable.

consumables.name: Aluminum oxide 36-60 grit (anti-slip aggregate for steps/ramps)
consumables.usage_rate: 1-2 LB per 100 SF of step/ramp area
consumables.notes: MANDATORY anti-slip aggregate for steps, ramps, and sloped areas where slip risk is elevated. Aluminum oxide is harder and more durable than silica sand — critical for high-traffic step nosings. 36-60 grit range. Required when has_steps = true or floor_slope > 0. Broadcast into wet coating. More aggressive texture than silica — not recommended for bare-foot comfort zones.

consumables.name: Cleanup rags / shop towels
consumables.notes: General cleanup rags for wiping edges, cleaning spills, and tool maintenance. Lint-free preferred for polyurea work. Dispose of solvent-soaked rags per local regulations — spontaneous combustion hazard with oil-based products.

consumables.name: Solvent for polyurea tool cleanup (xylene or acetone)
consumables.notes: For cleaning polyurea/polyaspartic product from tools, roller frames, and mixing equipment. Water will NOT clean polyurea — solvent is required. Xylene or acetone per manufacturer recommendation. Must clean tools IMMEDIATELY after use — cured polyurea cannot be removed. Polyurea coating_system only.

consumables.name: PPE kit for acid etch (gloves, goggles, respirator)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per crew member performing acid etch
consumables.notes: Chemical-resistant gloves (nitrile or neoprene), splash-proof safety goggles, and acid-rated half-face respirator with acid gas cartridges. MANDATORY for muriatic acid handling. Also required for acid stain application. OSHA CFR 1926.55 compliance.

consumables.name: Pin-type moisture meter (concrete verification tool)
consumables.notes: Electronic pin-type or surface moisture meter for concrete moisture verification. Supplement with ASTM D4263 plastic sheet test (taped to floor 16-24 hours, check for condensation). For critical applications (polyurea), ASTM F2170 in-situ RH probe is preferred. Essential for concrete porch floors on slab-on-grade without vapor barrier.

consumables.name: Stiff bristle scrub brush / push broom
consumables.notes: Heavy-duty stiff bristle push broom or deck scrub brush for working acid etch into concrete surface, scrubbing during cleaning, and agitating acid neutralizer. Poly or tampico bristle — not wire (wire can embed in concrete surface). Also useful for sweeping debris and dust before coating.

ext_wall_base_perimeter.description: Wall surfaces at floor-to-wall junction requiring splatter protection
ext_wall_base_perimeter.notes: Tape and paper at wall base where porch floor meets house wall, knee walls, or half walls. Roller application generates splatter that marks adjacent wall surfaces. 12-18 inch paper height above floor line.

ext_landscape_edge.description: Landscape and planting beds adjacent to porch perimeter
ext_landscape_edge.notes: Plastic sheeting along porch perimeter edge where landscaping is adjacent. Prevents coating drip from porch edge onto plantings. LF-based along perimeter.

ext_hardscape_adjacent.description: Adjacent walkways, driveway, or patio surfaces
ext_hardscape_adjacent.notes: Canvas drop cloths for non-slip crew traffic areas at porch entry. Plastic sheeting for protecting walkway and driveway surfaces from coating drip and roller splatter.

ext_railing_base.description: Railing post bases and column bases on porch floor
ext_railing_base.notes: Mask railing post bases and column bases where they meet the floor surface. Prevents coating from wicking up post base and creating unsightly buildup. Per post/column count.

ext_light_fixture.notes: Bag or tape over porch ceiling fixtures during floor coating. Floor-level roller splatter can reach ceiling fixtures on covered porches. Per fixture count.

compatibility_rules.description: Porch enamel on concrete requires alkali-resistant masonry primer
compatibility_rules.notes: New concrete pH 12-14 requires alkali-resistant primer. Standard acrylic primer will fail via saponification — alkaline hydroxides hydrolyze binder. Non-negotiable on bare concrete regardless of concrete age (even 28-day cured concrete remains alkaline).

compatibility_rules.description: Porch enamel on wood requires exterior wood primer
compatibility_rules.notes: Bare wood porch floor must be primed for adhesion and moisture sealing before porch enamel application. Mill glaze must be removed before priming.

compatibility_rules.description: Acrylic sealer is self-priming — no separate primer
compatibility_rules.notes: Acrylic concrete sealer is designed to penetrate and bond directly to profiled concrete. Adding a primer between concrete and sealer prevents proper sealer penetration and adhesion. Acid etch or mechanical profiling provides the adhesion profile.

compatibility_rules.description: Concrete stain requires sealer topcoat — stain alone is not traffic-rated
compatibility_rules.notes: Penetrating concrete stain has no film build and no abrasion resistance. Walking traffic will erode exposed stain rapidly. Clear acrylic topcoat sealer is MANDATORY to protect stain and provide wear surface. 2 coats of sealer for floor traffic durability.
Polyurea systems are proprietary — basecoat and topcoat must be from the same manufacturer. Cross-brand mixing causes intercoat adhesion failure. Verify system compatibility before procurement.

compatibility_rules.description: Failed moisture test triggers moisture mitigating primer (hard stop override)
compatibility_rules.notes: HARD STOP: If concrete moisture vapor emission rate exceeds 5 lbs per 1000 SF per 24 hours (ASTM F1869) or in-situ relative humidity exceeds 85% (ASTM F2170), moisture mitigating primer is mandatory BEFORE any other coating. This overrides all coating system primer selections. Coating over high-moisture concrete causes blistering, delamination, and total system failure.

compatibility_rules.description: Steps require aluminum oxide aggregate — silica sand insufficient
compatibility_rules.notes: Steps and ramps have elevated slip risk. Aluminum oxide is harder, more durable, and provides superior traction vs silica sand. Silica sand is acceptable for level floor field but NOT for steps. Code compliance (IBC/IRC) may require specific slip resistance coefficient on stairs.

compatibility_rules.description: Polyurea is concrete-only — BLOCKED on wood substrate
compatibility_rules.action: BLOCK — polyurea is not compatible with wood substrates
compatibility_rules.notes: Polyurea/polyaspartic coatings require mechanically profiled concrete (CSP 2-3) for adhesion. Wood substrate cannot achieve the required profile. Polyurea on wood will delaminate under thermal cycling and moisture movement. Redirect to porch_enamel for wood substrates.

compatibility_rules.description: Concrete stain is concrete-only — BLOCKED on wood substrate
compatibility_rules.action: BLOCK — concrete stain chemistry requires cementitious substrate
compatibility_rules.notes: Acid stain reacts with calcium hydroxide in concrete — no reaction occurs on wood. Water-based concrete stain is formulated for concrete porosity, not wood grain. Wood porch floors should use porch_enamel or a deck stain system (separate spec family).

compatibility_rules.description: Acrylic sealer is concrete-only — BLOCKED on wood substrate
compatibility_rules.action: BLOCK — acrylic concrete sealer is not formulated for wood substrates
compatibility_rules.notes: Acrylic concrete sealers are formulated for cementitious substrates. They do not penetrate or bond properly to wood grain. Wood porch floors should use porch_enamel for opaque coating or a deck stain/sealer system (separate spec family).

compatibility_rules.description: Anti-slip aggregate mandatory for ALL coating systems
compatibility_rules.notes: All porch floor coating systems MUST include anti-slip aggregate. Exterior horizontal walking surfaces become extremely slippery when wet without aggregate. Silica sand for level floor field, aluminum oxide for steps/ramps. Broadcast into wet first coat of finish/sealer/topcoat. Liability exposure for slip-and-fall on uncoated floors is significant.

compatibility_rules.description: Oil-based and alkyd products PROHIBITED on concrete substrates
compatibility_rules.required_chemistry: water-based acrylic, polyurea, or reactive stain only
compatibility_rules.notes: Alkaline concrete (pH 12-14) saponifies oil-based and alkyd binders. Same failure mechanism as masonry walls. All concrete porch floor systems in this spec are water-based acrylic or polyurea chemistry.

compatibility_rules.description: Acid etch profiling mandatory before coating on concrete (unless mechanically profiled)
compatibility_rules.required_action: Acid etch (muriatic acid 1:3 dilution) OR mechanical profiling (diamond grind/shot blast) to achieve CSP 2-3
compatibility_rules.notes: Smooth or cured concrete has insufficient surface profile for coating adhesion. Acid etch or mechanical profiling opens concrete pores and creates micro-texture (CSP 2-3) for mechanical bond. Polyurea specifically requires mechanical profiling — acid etch alone may be insufficient. Verify profile with CSP comparator chip.

risk_notes.topic: Moisture-driven coating failure on slab-on-grade concrete
risk_notes.risk: Exterior porch floors on slab-on-grade construction without proper vapor barrier are subject to moisture vapor transmission from below. Moisture migrating through concrete causes blistering, delamination, and whitening (efflorescence) of floor coatings. This is the #1 failure mode for concrete porch floor coatings.
risk_notes.mitigation: Moisture test per ASTM F1869 (calcium chloride) or ASTM F2170 (in-situ RH) before coating. MVER > 5 lbs = hard stop, requires SYS_EXT_PRFL_PRIMER_MOISTURE_MITIGATING. Supplemental ASTM D4263 plastic sheet test as field verification. Budget extra day for testing on concrete porch floor projects.

risk_notes.topic: Slip-and-fall liability on coated exterior floors
risk_notes.risk: Coated exterior porch floors become extremely slippery when wet (rain, dew, snow melt, irrigation). Smooth floor coatings without anti-slip aggregate create a significant slip-and-fall hazard. Liability exposure is high — exterior walking surfaces are subject to building code slip resistance requirements.
risk_notes.mitigation: Anti-slip aggregate is MANDATORY on all coating systems — no exceptions. Silica sand for level surfaces, aluminum oxide for steps/ramps. Verify aggregate distribution is uniform before coating skins. Document anti-slip application in project record.

risk_notes.risk: Muriatic acid (31.45% HCl) is a corrosive, toxic chemical that produces hydrochloric acid fumes. Skin contact causes chemical burns. Eye contact causes severe damage. Inhalation of fumes causes respiratory distress. Improper mixing (adding water to acid instead of acid to water) causes violent exothermic reaction and spattering.
risk_notes.mitigation: MANDATORY PPE: chemical-resistant gloves, splash goggles, acid-rated respirator. Always add acid to water. Work in well-ventilated area (exterior porches are inherently ventilated). Have water hose running and accessible for emergency rinse. Baking soda on hand for neutralization. First aid kit with eye wash station. OSHA CFR 1926.55 compliance.

risk_notes.topic: Polyurea pot life and application window constraints
risk_notes.risk: Two-component polyurea/polyaspartic products have extremely short pot life (15-30 minutes after mixing). Mixed product that is not applied within pot life gels in the container and is wasted. Application must be continuous and fast — stopping mid-application causes visible lap lines that cannot be corrected.
risk_notes.mitigation: Mix only what can be applied in 15 minutes. Pre-plan application path before mixing. Two-person crew minimum (one mixing, one applying). Temperature affects pot life — hotter = shorter. Do not attempt polyurea application without prior experience. Budget for material waste (10-15% of total) due to pot life constraints.

risk_notes.risk: Acid stain reacts chemically with calcium hydroxide in concrete — color result depends on concrete mix, age, porosity, and finishing method. Results are inherently mottled and variegated. Color cannot be precisely predicted or matched across pours. Customer expectation mismatch is common.
risk_notes.mitigation: Set customer expectations: acid stain produces unique, non-uniform color. Provide sample on inconspicuous area before full application. Document that color variation is inherent to the product, not a defect. Water-based concrete stain offers more predictable (but less dramatic) color if uniformity is priority.

risk_notes.topic: Porch enamel traffic wear on concrete
risk_notes.risk: Acrylic porch enamel on exterior concrete is subject to UV exposure, freeze-thaw cycling, and foot traffic abrasion. Expected maintenance cycle is 3-5 years depending on traffic volume and exposure. High-traffic entry porches wear faster at threshold and stair nosing.
risk_notes.mitigation: Set customer expectations for maintenance cycle. 2 coats minimum for durability. Anti-slip aggregate adds wear resistance. Touch-up high-wear areas at 2-3 years extends full recoat cycle. Polyurea system offers longer wear life (7-10 years) if budget allows.

risk_notes.topic: Wood porch floor moisture entrapment under paint film
risk_notes.risk: Painted wood porch floors trap moisture between wood and paint film. Moisture enters through board joints, end grain, fastener holes, and from below (if no ventilation beneath porch). Trapped moisture causes blistering, peeling, and accelerated wood rot. Horizontal surfaces collect more water than vertical — amplifying this failure mode.
risk_notes.mitigation: Ensure adequate ventilation beneath wood porch (open lattice or vented skirting). Seal end grain and board joints with extra primer coat. Verify wood MC < 15% before priming. Prime all six sides of replacement boards before installation when possible. Anti-slip aggregate in finish coat helps hide early wear.

coating_system_material_stacks.porch_enamel_concrete: 1 coat primer (250 SF/gal) + 2 coats enamel (350 SF/gal each). For 200 SF porch: ~0.8 gal primer + ~1.15 gal enamel = ~2 gal total. Add 10% waste.
coating_system_material_stacks.porch_enamel_wood: 1 coat primer (375 SF/gal) + 2 coats enamel (375 SF/gal each). For 200 SF porch: ~0.55 gal primer + ~1.07 gal enamel = ~1.6 gal total. Add 10% waste.
coating_system_material_stacks.acrylic_sealer: 2 coats sealer (250 SF/gal each). For 200 SF porch: ~1.6 gal sealer total. Self-priming. Add 10% waste.
coating_system_material_stacks.concrete_stain_acid: 1 coat acid stain (150 SF/gal) + 2 coats topcoat sealer (300 SF/gal each). For 200 SF porch: ~1.35 gal stain + ~1.35 gal sealer = ~2.7 gal total. Add 15% waste (acid stain is less predictable).
coating_system_material_stacks.concrete_stain_water: 2 coats water stain (250 SF/gal each) + 2 coats topcoat sealer (300 SF/gal each). For 200 SF porch: ~1.6 gal stain + ~1.35 gal sealer = ~2.95 gal total. Add 10% waste.
coating_system_material_stacks.polyurea: 1 coat basecoat primer (250 SF/gal) + 1 coat polyurea topcoat (175 SF/gal). For 200 SF porch: ~0.8 gal primer + ~1.15 gal topcoat = ~1.95 gal total. Add 15% waste (pot life constraints).

material_quantity_notes.anti_slip_aggregate_quantity: Silica sand: 1-2 lbs per 100 SF level floor. Aluminum oxide: 1-2 lbs per 100 SF steps/ramps. For 200 SF porch with 6 steps (~30 SF step area): ~3-4 lbs silica sand + ~0.5-1 lb aluminum oxide.
material_quantity_notes.acid_etch_material: Muriatic acid: 1 GAL concentrate per 75-100 SF (diluted 1:3). For 200 SF porch: ~2-3 GAL concentrate + ~1 box (5 lb) baking soda for neutralization.
material_quantity_notes.concrete_texture_factor: Smooth troweled: 1.00x. Broom finish: 1.15x. Heavy broom/exposed aggregate: 1.30x. Applied to all coating layers. Texture modifier increases material consumption on textured concrete.
material_quantity_notes.step_material_supplement: Steps add 15-25% material over calculated floor field due to: multiple small surfaces (tread, riser, nosing), edge cutting losses, and anti-slip aggregate (aluminum oxide) for each step. Budget 1 extra quart of coating per 4-6 steps.

assumptions.value: 200-300 SF/gal for alkali-resistant masonry primer on concrete floor
assumptions.note: Concrete floor coverage is comparable to masonry wall coverage. Floor application may be slightly lower due to horizontal pooling tendency. Broom-finish concrete reduces coverage 15-20% vs smooth.

assumptions.value: 300-400 SF/gal on concrete, 350-400 SF/gal on wood
assumptions.source: Manufacturer PDS (SW Porch & Floor Enamel); research.json
assumptions.note: Coverage rates derived from manufacturer product data sheets and confirmed by research findings. Concrete coverage varies by texture. Wood coverage is consistent on primed dimensional lumber.

assumptions.value: 150-200 SF/gal for topcoat, 200-300 SF/gal for basecoat
assumptions.note: Polyurea coverage is highly manufacturer-specific. Range represents typical residential-grade polyaspartic systems. Professional-grade systems may differ. Flag for field calibration with specific manufacturer system.

Acid stain coverage is the most variable of all systems due to reactive chemistry. Porosity, concrete age, and mix design all affect consumption. Conservative low-end (100 SF/gal) should be budgeted for estimating. Test application on sample area recommended.

Broadcast rate is an approximation. Actual rate depends on desired texture level and aggregate mesh size. Fine mesh (60) requires more weight for equivalent coverage vs coarse mesh (30-40). Field calibration needed.

assumptions.value: MVER > 5 lbs per 1000 SF per 24 hours OR RH > 85%
assumptions.source: ASTM F1869; ASTM F2170; industry standard thresholds
assumptions.note: Industry-standard moisture thresholds for floor coatings. Most coating manufacturers specify these thresholds in their product data sheets as maximum allowable moisture levels.

uncertainty_flags.description: Polyurea/polyaspartic coverage varies significantly between manufacturers and product lines. The 150-200 SF/gal range is typical but specific systems may fall outside this range. DFT requirements vary by manufacturer (8-12 mils typical, some systems specify 15-20 mils).
uncertainty_flags.impact: Material quantity estimates for polyurea could be off by 20-30%. Always confirm with specific manufacturer PDS before ordering.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Specify manufacturer system in project record. Use manufacturer-specific coverage rate for material ordering.

uncertainty_flags.description: Acid stain coverage on concrete is the most unpredictable of all coating systems. Coverage depends on concrete mix design (cement content, aggregate ratio), pour age, finishing method, and porosity — factors that are not known until application begins.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Material ordering for acid stain projects should budget 25-50% overage. Under-ordering causes mid-project procurement delays and potential color lot mismatch.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Test application on 25-50 SF sample area to calibrate actual coverage before ordering full quantity.

uncertainty_flags.description: Anti-slip aggregate durability on exterior walking surfaces is not well-documented. Silica sand may erode from traffic and weathering faster than aluminum oxide. Reapplication cycle is unknown — may require periodic recoating to maintain slip resistance.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Customer expectations for slip resistance longevity may exceed actual performance. Maintenance recoating may be needed at 2-3 year intervals to refresh aggregate.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Field data on aggregate durability at 1, 3, and 5 year intervals across coating systems.
